name: Fergal Nolan
backstory: The good biscuit tin still sits on top of the fridge, empty, because he has never let anything go back into it. He grew up knowing exactly what things cost and who had to pay for them, and he has not forgotten a single price. He refuses himself the things he wants, a decent coat, the holiday his partner keeps raising, a car that doesn't rattle, because spending on himself feels like taking from people who had nothing. Being looked down on bothers him more than going without. He wants the school gates to open at the same time every morning, the mantel clock wound, the same faces at the same table, and he takes it personally when his children grow or his partner wants something new. The secret is a list in biro, at the back of an old school diary, of everyone who has cheated, belittled or let him down. He adds to it and reads it when he is alone. No one has seen it, and no one is meant to.
persona: He runs the school site the way he always has, and waves off any new ideas as fancy notions nobody asked for. His car is spotless and his shoes are polished, and visitors will be shown what he has bought before they leave. He is loyal to the few people he trusts and keeps a long memory for anyone who has crossed him. He will argue until someone gives in, and he has no interest in paintings or views.
speaking_style: Slow and measured, in plain short sentences with no slang. He repeats a point rather than raising his voice, and when he is cornered he falls back on how things have always been done. Under his breath he hums three bars of a hymn.

past.content: A split ran down the back of my only coat. Buying a new one felt worse than the cold, so I wore it through two winters, and the jumper someone gave me is still in the drawer with the tags on.
We were out at the pictures in town when the back door was forced. When we got home the cash was gone from the biscuit tin, and the tin was lying on the kitchen floor.
The first night the child was in the house, they wouldn't let go of my sleeve. I sat on the landing floor with my back to the wall until their breathing slowed, and I stayed there until it did.

hooks.description: Behind the bins at the end of a shift, I watched them take a brown envelope from someone in a grey van. I haven't said a word, and I'm not sure why.
They borrowed three hundred pounds to cover a bill and promised it back by the end of the month. Every time I've brought it up since, they've found somewhere else to be.
I pulled them out of the river when they went under. I never told anyone, because I didn't want to be thanked for it.
We were inseparable all through school, then they left without a word. I still catch myself searching the faces in the café for them.

voice.description: A local accent, with nothing of anywhere else in it. A man in his late thirties. Mid-range pitch with a dry, level timbre; unhurried, deliberate delivery, with clear consonants and little lift at the end of lines. Measured and matter-of-fact, the manner of someone repeating a point he has already settled.
voice.reference_line: The boilers are serviced on the first Monday of each month, and the logbook is kept in the cupboard by the stage door.
